> **Time:** about 8 minutes. **Data:** a small synthetic SIRUP object bundled with SIRUP. **Needs:** SIRUP with spdep.

This page helps you pick a spatial statistic. Start from the question you ask, not from the function name. Each section below names one question. It then gives the function, the input, and the way to read the result. A *spot* is one capture location of the spatial assay. A *clone* is a group of receptors that descend from one ancestor cell.

All tests need a SIRUP object, or a Seurat object with spatial images. The tests read the spot coordinates from the object. Most tests compare each spot with its neighbors. You set the neighbors with `k` (the number of nearest spots) or `radius`. `vignette("spatial-statistics", package = "SIRUP")` runs every test on real data.

## Match the question to the function

| Question | Function | Input |
|---|---|---|
| Is this gene or cell type clustered? | `spatialMoran()` | One gene or numeric metadata column |
| Where are the clusters? | `spatialLocalMoran()` | The same input |
| Do two genes or cell types co-vary? | `spatialLee()` | Two continuous variables |
| Do spots of type A sit near spots of type B? | `spatialRipleyCrossK()` | One metadata column with two labels |
| Does one clone stay together? | `spatialCloneJoinCount()` | Receptor table with clone IDs |
| How far does a clone spread? | `spatialCloneSpread()` | Receptor table with clone IDs |
| How does the repertoire differ between regions? | Polygon summaries | Stored polygons |

## Ask whether a variable clusters

Use `spatialMoran()` to ask if neighboring spots have similar values. The function computes Moran's I. This statistic is near 0 when the values show no spatial pattern. It is positive when similar values sit together. It is negative when values alternate.

The input is one variable. `variable_type` says what it is: a gene (`"feature"`), a numeric metadata column (`"metadata"`), receptor presence (`"receptor"`), or one clone (`"clone"`). For a text metadata column, give `value` to test one level.

Read $I$ as the size of the pattern. Read the p value as the evidence for it. A large section gives a tiny p value for a weak pattern.

`spatialLocalMoran()` answers the next question: where are the clusters? It gives one value for each spot, with a z-score and a p value. Each spot has its own p value, so adjust for multiple testing. `plotSpatialLocalMoran()` draws the result on the tissue.

This chunk tests one gene on the synthetic object:

```{r moran}
library(SIRUP)
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
moran <- spatialMoran(x, variable = "gene1", k = 4)
moran$test$estimate[[1]]
moran$test$p.value
```

## Ask whether two variables co-vary

Use `spatialLee()` to ask if two continuous variables share a spatial pattern. Lee's L combines Pearson correlation with spatial smoothing. L is high when both variables are high in the same neighborhoods. The variables do not need to peak in the same spots.

The input is two continuous variables. Each can be a gene or a numeric metadata column. Give `x_type`, `y_type`, `assay`, and `layer` as needed. The result holds `L` and a test. The default test is analytical. It builds a dense matrix with one entry for each pair of spots. For large data, such as Visium HD, set `method = "mc"` to use permutations.

Run a positive control. Pick two genes that you expect to share a pattern. If the control fails, the data or the neighbor setting may be wrong.

## Ask whether two spot types sit near each other

Use `spatialRipleyCrossK()` to ask if spots of type A lie near spots of type B. The function counts the type B spots within each distance of an average type A spot. It compares the curve with curves from random relabeling.

The input is one metadata column that holds the labels. Give the two levels as `i` and `j`. Set `nsim` above 0 to get the envelope. Spots with `NA` in the column are left out.

Read the curve against the envelope. A curve above the envelope means A and B sit closer than chance. A curve below the envelope means each type groups with itself. Use `plotRipleyCrossK()` to draw it.

The distance is in image pixels at the stored `image_scale`. Convert it before you quote a distance in micrometers.

## Ask whether a clone stays together

Use `spatialCloneJoinCount()` to ask if the spots of one clone sit next to each other. The function marks the spots that hold the clone. It counts neighbor pairs in which both spots hold the clone. It then calls `spdep::joincount.test()`.

The input is a receptor table with clone IDs and spatial IDs. A SIRUP object holds both. By default, the function tests every clone that occurs in at least `min_spatial_ids` spots. Give `clone_val` to test chosen clones. If the object has stored polygons, the function runs one test for each polygon. Set `use_stored_polygons = FALSE` for one test over the section.

The summary table has one row for each clone. A high `statistic` (a z-score) and a small `p_value` mean that the clone stays together. The default alternative is `"greater"`, so the test looks for more joins than chance.

Moran's I also accepts one clone with `variable_type = "clone"`. It treats the clone as a 0/1 value for each spot. The join-count test is the first choice for clones.

## Ask how far a clone spreads

Use `spatialCloneSpread()` to measure the reach of a clone. It is a description, not a test. The function reports the mean and the maximum distance between the points of each clone, for each sample.

```{r spread}
spatialCloneSpread(x)
```

The input is a receptor table with clone IDs and spatial IDs. A clone needs at least `min_spatial_ids` points (default 2). By default, each sequence is a point, so sequences in the same spot give distances of 0. Set `collapse_within_spot = TRUE` to count each spot once. Distances are in image pixels.

## Compare regions with polygon summaries

The questions above treat the section as one field. To compare regions that you drew, use the polygon functions. `polygonReceptorSummary()` counts receptors, spots, and clones in each polygon. `spatialCloneDominance()` gives the fraction of receptors in each clone of each polygon. `polygonDiversity()` gives Hill diversity curves, rarefied to one size. These functions describe each region. They do not test a spatial pattern. `polygonDiversity()` leaves out polygons with fewer than `min_n` receptors.

For the full workflow, see `vignette("regions", package = "SIRUP")`.
